attribution: Original bounded CSS Vista skills teaching. Hypothetical examples are not evidence of real events. Grammar rules link to the existing course.

lessons.title: A complete sentence
lessons.explanation: A sentence expresses a complete thought. Find who or what the sentence is about, then what that subject does or is. An imperative may have an understood subject: you.
lessons.example: The researcher checked the figures. Subject: the researcher. Predicate: checked the figures.

check.prompt: Which sentence expresses a complete thought?
options: The committee published its report.
Because the report was late.
The report on the desk.
After checking the figures.
check.explanation: The subject committee has a finite verb, published, and the thought is complete.

lessons.task: Write one sentence about an action you completed today. Underline the subject mentally and identify its verb.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Subject and predicate
lessons.explanation: The subject identifies the person or thing discussed. The predicate says something about it. Extra words inside a subject do not change its head noun.
lessons.example: The books on the upper shelf belong to Sara. Books is the head noun; belong to Sara is the predicate.

check.prompt: Which is the head of the subject in "The quality of the reports matters"?
options: matters
of
quality
reports
check.explanation: Quality is the head noun; of the reports describes it.

lessons.task: Write a sentence whose subject includes an of phrase. Make the verb agree with the head noun.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Simple, compound and complex sentences
lessons.explanation: A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound sentence joins independent clauses. A complex sentence includes an independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Length alone does not determine the type.
lessons.example: The class ended, but the students stayed. Both clauses can stand alone.

check.prompt: Which example is complex?
options: The students stayed.
The class ended, and the students stayed.
The attentive students stayed quietly.
Although the class ended, the students stayed.
check.explanation: Although introduces a dependent clause; the students stayed is independent.

lessons.task: Write a simple sentence, then revise it to show a condition using if or a contrast using although.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Repairing fragments
lessons.explanation: A dependent clause cannot normally stand alone in formal prose. Attach it to an independent clause, or remove the dependency while preserving meaning.
lessons.example: Fragment: Because the road was closed. Complete: We returned because the road was closed.

check.prompt: Which repair is complete?
options: The closed road near the village.
Although the road was closed.
We postponed the visit because the road was closed.
Because the road was closed.
check.explanation: The repair supplies an independent clause with a subject and a finite verb.

lessons.task: Repair this fragment in your own way: "Although the proposal was promising." Do not invent evidence about a real proposal.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Run-ons and comma splices
lessons.explanation: Two independent clauses need suitable punctuation or a conjunction. A comma alone usually cannot join them. Choose a boundary that reflects their relationship.
lessons.example: Comma splice: The room was crowded, we waited outside. Repair: The room was crowded, so we waited outside.

check.prompt: Which punctuation joins two related independent clauses correctly?
options: The draft is ready, the editor will review it.
The draft is ready the editor will review it.
The draft is ready; because the editor will review it.
The draft is ready; the editor will review it.
check.explanation: A semicolon can connect closely related independent clauses.

lessons.task: Repair "The instructions were unclear, we asked for help" using a connector that shows the relationship.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Subject–verb agreement
lessons.explanation: Match the verb to the head of the subject. A nearby plural noun inside a describing phrase does not make a singular subject plural.
lessons.example: The list of supplies is complete. List is singular.

check.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The purpose of these meetings are clear.
The purposes of this meeting is clear.
The purpose of these meetings were clear.
The purpose of these meetings is clear.
check.explanation: The singular head purpose requires is in this present-tense sentence.

lessons.task: Write a sentence beginning "The value of these lessons" and complete it with an appropriate verb.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Tense consistency
lessons.explanation: Keep the time frame clear. Tenses may change when the time changes, but an unexplained switch confuses the sequence.
lessons.example: Yesterday I revised the outline and checked the references. Both actions belong to yesterday.

check.prompt: Which sentence keeps its stated past time frame?
options: Last night, she draft the paragraph and review it.
Last night, she drafted the paragraph and reviewed it.
Last night, she drafts the paragraph and reviewed it.
Last night, she drafted the paragraph and reviews it.
check.explanation: Drafted and reviewed both refer to the stated past period.

lessons.task: Describe two actions you completed yesterday in one sentence. Keep both verbs consistent with that time.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Clear word order
lessons.explanation: Put words near what they describe. Keep the main subject and verb easy to locate. Position only carefully because it can limit different parts of a sentence.
lessons.example: Only Mina submitted a draft means nobody else did. Mina submitted only a draft means she submitted nothing else.

check.prompt: Which sentence places only immediately before the submitted item?
options: Mina only submitted a draft.
Mina submitted a draft only to the editor.
Mina submitted only a draft.
Only Mina submitted a draft.
check.explanation: Only directly before a draft limits the item submitted.

lessons.task: Write two sentences with only in different positions, then explain how their meanings differ.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Misplaced and dangling modifiers
lessons.explanation: An opening participial phrase should describe the subject that follows. Otherwise the sentence may appear to assign an action to an object.
lessons.example: Dangling: Walking to class, the rain soaked me. Clear: Walking to class, I was soaked by the rain.

check.prompt: Which sentence avoids a dangling modifier?
options: After reviewing the figures, the report seemed clearer.
After reviewing the figures, the researcher corrected the table.
After reviewing the figures, the table was corrected.
After reviewing the figures, several errors appeared.
check.explanation: The researcher is the person who reviewed the figures.

lessons.task: Repair "After reading the instructions, the task became easier" by naming the person who read.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Parallel structure
lessons.explanation: Use matching grammatical forms for ideas presented as equals. Parallel structure helps readers recognize the relationship without reinterpreting the syntax.
lessons.example: The workshop teaches planning, drafting and revising. Each item is an -ing form.

check.prompt: Which list is parallel?
options: We aim to improving access, reduce delays and explain decisions.
We aim to improve access, delays and explaining decisions.
We aim to improve access, reduce delays and explain decisions.
We aim to improve access, reducing delays and decisions explained.
check.explanation: The coordinated verbs improve, reduce and explain share the same to.

lessons.task: Rewrite "The programme encourages reading, to discuss ideas and revision" with matching forms.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Cause, contrast and condition
lessons.explanation: Choose a connector that expresses the intended logic. Because gives a reason; although introduces contrast; if introduces a condition. These relationships are not interchangeable.
lessons.example: If the library extends its hours, more evening study may be possible. This is conditional, not a promise.

check.prompt: Which connector introduces a condition?
options: because
although
therefore
if
check.explanation: If sets a condition on the following claim.

lessons.task: Write three short sentences about a hypothetical study plan: one cause, one contrast and one condition.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Connectors and transitions
lessons.explanation: A transition must match the relationship between ideas. However signals contrast; therefore signals a conclusion; for example introduces an illustration. Punctuation still needs to be correct.
lessons.example: The first route is shorter. However, the second route has fewer obstacles.

check.prompt: Which transition best signals an illustration?
options: for example
nevertheless
therefore
in contrast
check.explanation: For example introduces an instance of the preceding general idea.

lessons.task: Write a general statement about a study habit and add an illustrative sentence with an appropriate transition.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Concision and redundancy
lessons.explanation: Remove words that repeat a meaning without removing necessary conditions or distinctions. Concision is faithful compression, not merely making a sentence shorter.
lessons.example: At this point in time can usually become now. A future possibility can often become a possibility.

check.prompt: Which revision keeps the meaning of "The reason for the delay is that the file is missing"?
options: The file is missing, causing the delay.
The file is missing.
The delay is unreasonable.
The file was destroyed.
check.explanation: The revision retains both the missing file and its stated causal relationship to the delay.

lessons.task: Shorten "It is necessary for students to make a plan in advance before they begin" without losing its instruction.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Clarity and precision
lessons.explanation: Identify what vague words refer to. Replace a vague noun or pronoun when the context permits, but do not manufacture details the writer has not supplied.
lessons.example: Vague: This improved things. Clear, with known context: The new timetable reduced missed classes.

check.prompt: What should an editor do when "this" has no clear referent?
options: Replace it with a statistic.
Assume the preceding person is meant.
Ask which idea or action the writer means.
Invent a likely policy.
check.explanation: Clarification preserves the writer’s meaning instead of inventing it.

lessons.task: Write a vague sentence with this or things, then replace the vague expression using only details you actually intend.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Word choice and academic tone
lessons.explanation: Use accurate, proportionate wording. Formal writing does not require rare words or hostility. Avoid absolute labels when your evidence supports only a qualified criticism.
lessons.example: Overstated: The proposal is totally useless. Precise: The proposal does not address the stated implementation problem.

check.prompt: Which option offers a measured criticism?
options: The argument overlooks the cost of implementation.
The argument is completely stupid.
Nobody could ever support the argument.
The argument proves that every reform fails.
check.explanation: The criticism identifies a specific limitation without personal insult or an unsupported universal claim.

lessons.task: Rewrite "This idea is really bad" as a specific criticism of a hypothetical idea, clearly stating the limitation.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Expressing cause and effect
lessons.explanation: Separate an observed association from a causal explanation. State the proposed mechanism and relevant condition. Use can or may when the claim is conditional.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: If unclear instructions delay decisions, clarifying responsibilities may reduce that delay.

check.prompt: Which sentence makes a conditional causal claim?
options: Two changes occurred together, so one must cause the other.
Decisions and responsibilities are the same thing.
Unclear responsibilities may delay decisions when approvals are required from several offices.
Unclear responsibilities always destroy all institutions.
check.explanation: The sentence proposes an outcome and a condition without claiming inevitability.

lessons.task: Construct a causal sentence about a hypothetical administrative delay. Include a mechanism and a qualification.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Building an argumentative sentence
lessons.explanation: Make a defensible claim, give a relevant reason and indicate the condition under which it applies. A strong sentence does more than announce a preference.
lessons.example: A trial of extended study hours is worth considering if evening access is a barrier, because it would test whether access improves attendance.

check.prompt: Which sentence gives a claim supported by relevant reasoning?
options: The timetable should be reviewed because it should be reviewed.
Everyone knows the timetable is wrong.
The timetable should be reviewed because two compulsory classes currently overlap.
The timetable should be reviewed because blue is a pleasant colour.
check.explanation: Overlapping compulsory classes is a relevant reason for reviewing a timetable.

lessons.task: Write a claim about a hypothetical classroom improvement and support it with one relevant reason.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Building an analytical sentence
lessons.explanation: Show how or why an outcome could arise. Name a mechanism, condition or competing explanation. Description tells what; analysis examines the relationship.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: A longer journey could reduce attendance by making punctual arrival harder, although class timing might also explain absences.

check.prompt: Which statement offers analysis rather than only description?
options: The library opens at a fixed time.
The library has a door.
Some students use the library.
A fixed opening time may restrict access for students whose classes finish later.
check.explanation: It links opening time to a possible mechanism affecting a defined group.

lessons.task: Write one analytical sentence about a hypothetical access problem, including an alternative explanation.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Qualification without vagueness
lessons.explanation: A qualification states the scope or condition of a claim. It should make the statement more precise rather than weaken every verb with several uncertain expressions.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: The shorter route is preferable when travel time matters more than shelter.

check.prompt: Which statement has a clear condition?
options: The shorter route is preferable when both routes are equally safe.
The shorter route is maybe perhaps sort of preferable.
The shorter route is always perfect for everyone.
The shorter route proves everything about travel.
check.explanation: The condition specifies the circumstances in which the comparison holds.

lessons.task: Make "Online discussion improves participation" into a qualified hypothesis without inventing supporting data.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Advanced sentence transformation
lessons.explanation: Change structure while preserving who acts, what is claimed, the time frame and qualifications. A passive construction or compressed clause must not strengthen the original claim.
lessons.example: Original: The team may finish the review if the missing files arrive. Equivalent: The review may be finished by the team if the missing files arrive.

check.prompt: Which revision preserves "The measure may reduce delays if staff receive training"?
options: Training has already eliminated delays.
The measure reduces delays without any conditions.
With staff training, the measure may reduce delays.
The measure will eliminate delays.
check.explanation: May and the training condition remain; neither certainty nor timing is invented.

lessons.task: Transform a conditional sentence of your own into a different structure. Check that its qualification and meaning survive.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and word choice
lessons.explanation: Choose words for their meaning and natural use in context. Similar dictionary meanings do not make words interchangeable. Check what a replacement would add, remove or imply.
lessons.example: Effective concerns achieving an intended result; efficient concerns the resources used. A measure may be effective but costly. Decide which judgement you intend before choosing either word.

check.prompt: Which sentence preserves the meaning "These figures do not provide enough support for the claim"?
options: These figures are significant.
These figures are insufficient to support the claim.
These figures disprove the claim.
These figures confirm the claim.
check.explanation: Insufficient means not enough. Lack of enough support does not establish that the opposite claim is true.

lessons.task: Write a sentence using effective or efficient. Explain the meaning you intend and test an alternative word against it.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Fact, opinion and argument
lessons.explanation: A factual claim can be checked; an opinion expresses a judgement; an argument offers reasons for a conclusion. A factual-looking claim may still be unverified.
lessons.example: Hypothetical opinion: I prefer longer library hours. Argument: The library should trial longer hours because some classes end after it closes.

check.prompt: Which is an argument?
options: The timetable should change because two required classes overlap.
I like the timetable.
The timetable contains eight entries.
The timetable is printed on paper.
check.explanation: The timetable proposal gives a conclusion and a relevant reason.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Finding a central claim
lessons.explanation: A central claim states what you want a reader to accept. Keep it specific enough to challenge and distinguish it from the topic.
lessons.example: Topic: classroom access. Claim: A trial evening session could improve access for students with late classes.

check.prompt: Which is a claim rather than only a topic?
options: Different schedules.
The school should trial an evening study session.
Evening study.
School buildings.
check.explanation: The sentence proposes a position that can be supported or challenged.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Relevant supporting reasons
lessons.explanation: A reason supports a claim only when it helps explain why the conclusion should be accepted. A true but unrelated statement is not useful support.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: Repairing a broken light is relevant to safe evening use; the colour of the noticeboard is not.

check.prompt: Which reason is relevant to repairing a broken classroom light?
options: The school logo has three colours.
The headteacher likes music.
The timetable was printed yesterday.
Students cannot read the board clearly in that room.
check.explanation: Visibility bears directly on the purpose of the repair.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Explaining the link
lessons.explanation: Explain the link between the reason and the claim. Naming two ideas beside each other does not show why one supports the other.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: Moving a class avoids the overlap, so students can attend both required sessions.

check.prompt: Which sentence explains the reason–claim link?
options: The overlap and class exist.
Everyone wants a change.
Moving one class would remove the overlap and allow attendance at both.
The class should move because moving is good.
check.explanation: It names the mechanism by which the proposed change helps.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Selecting evidence
lessons.explanation: Choose evidence that bears on the claim and has an identifiable source, date and scope. An illustrative example is not proof of a general claim.
lessons.example: To examine library access, collect opening times and actual student schedules; a fictional example only explains the question.

check.prompt: Which evidence is most directly relevant to a claimed timetable overlap?
options: The dated timetables for both required classes.
A quotation about courage.
An unrelated national statistic.
An anonymous preference for shorter lessons.
check.explanation: The actual timetables can establish whether those class times overlap.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Premises and conclusions
lessons.explanation: Premises are the supporting statements; the conclusion is what they are meant to establish. Check whether accepting the premises really supports that conclusion.
lessons.example: All required classes must be attendable. Two required classes overlap. Therefore, the timetable needs review. This identifies a conflict, without proving a particular remedy.

check.prompt: What is the conclusion in that example?
options: Classes exist.
The timetable needs review.
Two required classes overlap.
All required classes must be attendable.
check.explanation: Needs review is the judgement supported by the premises.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Identifying assumptions
lessons.explanation: An assumption is a step your reasoning relies on without establishing it. Name it and ask what happens if it is false.
lessons.example: A longer opening period will help only if affected students can and wish to use it.

check.prompt: Which assumption needs checking before an evening-access trial?
options: The notice is printed on paper.
Every student has identical needs.
Longer hours can never have costs.
Affected students can use the proposed evening hours.
check.explanation: Potential access depends on whether the relevant students can actually attend.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Cause-and-effect arguments
lessons.explanation: A causal argument needs a mechanism, timing and consideration of alternative causes. Events occurring together do not by themselves establish causation.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: If unclear approval responsibility delays a task, naming a responsible officer may reduce that delay.

check.prompt: Why is "attendance rose after the notice, so the notice caused the rise" incomplete?
options: Other changes could explain the rise.
Every later event proves causation.
Timing never matters.
No causal claim can ever be tested.
check.explanation: The sequence is compatible with causation but does not exclude other explanations.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Recognising common fallacies
lessons.explanation: A personal attack does not refute reasoning. A false dilemma excludes alternatives without justification. Circular reasoning restates the claim as its reason.
lessons.example: Circular: This plan is best because no plan is better. That supplies no independent support.

check.prompt: Which statement is circular?
options: The rule is justified because it is a justified rule.
The rule needs review because it conflicts with another requirement.
There may be a third option.
The conclusion needs supporting evidence.
check.explanation: The reason merely repeats the conclusion.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Weak and irrelevant arguments
lessons.explanation: Separate a reason that fails from a conclusion that may still be true. Rejecting one bad argument does not automatically prove the opposite conclusion.
lessons.example: An irrelevant colour preference does not support extending library hours, but it does not prove that hours should remain unchanged.

check.prompt: What follows when a reason is irrelevant?
options: The opposite claim is certainly true.
Every argument on the topic is false.
The person must be dishonest.
That reason does not support the claim.
check.explanation: Failure of support is not proof of the opposite position.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Constructing a counterargument
lessons.explanation: Present a serious opposing reason in a form an informed opponent might accept. Do not make the opposing view weaker for convenience.
lessons.example: A concern about longer library hours could be staffing cost and the reliability of supervision.

check.prompt: Which counterargument engages an access proposal seriously?
options: Longer hours may require staffing resources that are unavailable.
Opponents hate students.
Nobody should ever use libraries.
The proposal has words in it.
check.explanation: It identifies a practical constraint relevant to the proposal.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Responding with a rebuttal
lessons.explanation: Answer the actual opposing reason. Concede what is valid, show what evidence is needed and explain why your position remains defensible under stated conditions.
lessons.example: A limited trial could test demand within an agreed staffing budget; it cannot guarantee that costs disappear.

check.prompt: Which reply addresses a staffing-cost objection?
options: Claim all staff work for free.
Attack the objector personally.
Trial limited hours within a stated budget, then compare demand and cost.
Ignore the cost because the idea is popular.
check.explanation: The reply directly addresses the constraint and proposes a test rather than inventing savings.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Qualification and nuance
lessons.explanation: State where your claim applies and where it may fail. A qualified claim can be stronger because its scope matches its reasons and evidence.
lessons.example: A trial is defensible if supervision and staffing are available; otherwise another access arrangement may be preferable.

check.prompt: Which claim is appropriately qualified?
options: Every trial is always successful.
All alternatives are impossible.
Success is guaranteed without evidence.
A trial may be useful where staffing and demand justify it.
check.explanation: The qualification connects the claim to relevant conditions.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Developing an argumentative paragraph
lessons.explanation: Organise a paragraph around one claim, explain the reason, identify suitable evidence and relate it back to the claim. Avoid a list of disconnected slogans.
lessons.example: Plan: claim about access → mechanism → evidence needed → limitation → qualified conclusion. This is a structure, not a supplied argument.

check.prompt: Which item should explain why evidence supports the claim?
options: A longer title.
A repeated slogan.
The reasoning linking the evidence to the claim.
An unrelated anecdote.
check.explanation: Readers need the inferential connection, not merely a pasted fact.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Evaluating a complete argument
lessons.explanation: Review relevance, clarity, logical consistency, reasoning, evidence, alternatives, rebuttal and coherence. These instructional criteria are not examiner marks.
lessons.example: A defensible argument may still need better evidence; do not confuse fluent language with a sound inference.

check.prompt: Which review is most useful?
options: Assign an unexplained precise percentage.
Praise length alone.
Assume polished wording proves the claim.
Identify a specific inference or evidence gap and explain how to test it.
check.explanation: Specific criticism helps the writer revise a real weakness.

lessons.task: Develop your own position on whether a hypothetical school should trial evening library hours. Apply this lesson’s focus, or choose your own statement.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Description and analysis
lessons.explanation: Description states what happens. Analysis examines how, why or under what conditions it happens. Neither permits inventing evidence.
lessons.example: Description: A school uses an online form. Analysis question: How could the form change the time needed to process a request?

check.prompt: Which question is analytical?
options: Where is its title printed?
How might the form alter processing time?
What colour is the form?
What is the form called?
check.explanation: It asks about a mechanism connecting a change to an outcome.

lessons.task: Analyse the hypothetical statement: unclear administrative responsibilities can delay decisions. Explain mechanisms, conditions and alternatives, or enter an issue of your own.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Causes and consequences
lessons.explanation: Separate a proposed cause from its consequences. Explain the intermediate steps, then identify what would need checking.
lessons.example: Hypothetical chain: unclear instructions → repeated queries → delayed completion. Each link needs evidence.

check.prompt: What should be added to a list of causes?
options: A guarantee that the list is complete.
An explanation of how each could produce the outcome.
An invented statistic.
An assertion that all causes are equal.
check.explanation: Analysis explains links rather than merely naming possible causes.

lessons.task: Analyse the hypothetical statement: unclear administrative responsibilities can delay decisions. Explain mechanisms, conditions and alternatives, or enter an issue of your own.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Relationships between variables
lessons.explanation: A variable is a quantity or characteristic that can differ. Ask how a change in one might relate to another, and whether conditions alter that relationship.
lessons.example: Hypothetical variables: travel time and attendance. A relationship could differ with transport reliability.

check.prompt: Which pair can frame an access analysis?
options: The same word repeated twice.
A conclusion without any variables.
An unrelated personal insult.
Travel time and attendance.
check.explanation: The pair allows a relationship to be examined rather than assumed.

lessons.task: Analyse the hypothetical statement: unclear administrative responsibilities can delay decisions. Explain mechanisms, conditions and alternatives, or enter an issue of your own.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Recognising assumptions
lessons.explanation: Identify a step taken for granted. Ask whether it is necessary and what evidence could support or challenge it.
lessons.example: An online service helps only if users have the access and skills needed to use it.

check.prompt: What assumption underlies a claim that online forms improve everyone’s access?
options: Everyone concerned can access and use the form.
The form has a name.
No service has a user.
Every form is a printed book.
check.explanation: The universal claim relies on access and usability, which need checking.

lessons.task: Analyse the hypothetical statement: unclear administrative responsibilities can delay decisions. Explain mechanisms, conditions and alternatives, or enter an issue of your own.

lessons.title: Evaluating evidence
lessons.explanation: Consider source, date, method, population and relevance. A small self-selected response does not automatically represent everyone.
lessons.example: A voluntary class survey may reveal respondents’ views but cannot alone establish the whole school’s preferences.

check.prompt: What limitation should be noted for a voluntary survey?
options: Every respondent must be lying.
The survey proves the views of everyone.
Dates and sample selection never matter.
Respondents may differ from nonrespondents.
check.explanation: Selection can affect what the findings represent.

lessons.title: Competing explanations
lessons.explanation: Develop plausible alternatives and ask what observations could distinguish them. Do not list alternatives and then ignore them.
lessons.example: Absence could relate to travel, class timing or illness; different records would help distinguish these explanations.

check.prompt: What makes an alternative explanation useful?
options: A clear prediction that can be compared with observations.
Its ability to sound complicated.
A made-up citation.
Its repetition of the first explanation.
check.explanation: A discriminating prediction helps test competing explanations.

lessons.title: Correlation and causation
lessons.explanation: Association does not establish causal direction or exclude a third factor. Examine mechanism, sequence and competing explanations.
lessons.example: Two outcomes might both change after a timetable revision; this does not alone show that one caused the other.

check.prompt: What could explain an observed association besides direct causation?
options: All observations must be fabricated.
Mechanisms cannot matter.
A third factor affecting both variables.
The association is necessarily proof.
check.explanation: A common cause can produce association without direct causation between the measured variables.

lessons.title: Institutional and structural factors
lessons.explanation: Look beyond individual intention to rules, resources, responsibilities and incentives. These factors are possible explanations, not excuses or automatic causes.
lessons.example: A request may wait because no office has a clear approval responsibility, even when individuals want to help.

check.prompt: Which is an institutional factor?
options: A person’s favourite colour.
An unrelated weather description.
A nickname for the office.
The rule assigning approval responsibility.
check.explanation: The rule governs how the institution processes decisions.

lessons.title: Analysing multiple dimensions
lessons.explanation: Choose dimensions relevant to the issue: resources, implementation, distribution, incentives or rights. More headings do not help unless each affects the reasoning.
lessons.example: A hypothetical education initiative can be examined for access, teaching capacity, cost and unequal effects.

check.prompt: When should a dimension be included?
options: Even when it has no connection to the issue.
When it changes an explanation, consequence or judgement.
Whenever it makes the answer longer.
Only because it sounds academic.
check.explanation: Relevant dimensions deepen reasoning; unrelated headings add clutter.

lessons.title: Short- and long-term implications
lessons.explanation: Separate immediate effects from effects that depend on adaptation, maintenance or changed incentives. State uncertainty about future outcomes.
lessons.example: A new system may take training time now and might reduce repeated work later; both claims need evidence.

check.prompt: Which comparison distinguishes time horizons?
options: An unrelated comparison of colours.
Initial training costs versus possible later processing gains.
Two names for the same moment.
A guarantee about all future outcomes.
check.explanation: It compares immediate demands with outcomes that could emerge later.

lessons.title: Identifying trade-offs
lessons.explanation: A trade-off arises when improving one objective can constrain another. Explain what is gained, what may be lost and who bears the consequences.
lessons.example: Longer opening hours may improve access but require more staffing or a narrower range of services.

check.prompt: Which question tests a trade-off?
options: Can we assume unlimited resources?
Is every cost imaginary?
Can the title be longer?
What other service might lose resources if hours are extended?
check.explanation: It examines an opportunity cost relevant to the decision.

lessons.title: Counterfactual thinking
lessons.explanation: A counterfactual asks what might happen without the proposed cause or intervention. It helps distinguish the effect of a change from an existing trend.
lessons.example: To assess a new timetable, ask how attendance might have changed under the previous timetable over the same period.

check.prompt: What is the relevant counterfactual?
options: Attendance during that period if the timetable had not changed.
Attendance after the change only.
An unrelated school’s name.
The assumption that attendance cannot change.
check.explanation: The comparison concerns the outcome in the absence of the change.

lessons.title: Comparing proposed solutions
lessons.explanation: Apply consistent criteria such as feasibility, cost, access and unintended effects. State the evidence and assumptions behind each comparison.
lessons.example: Compare a later opening time with an evening trial using the same access and staffing criteria.

check.prompt: What makes a comparison fair?
options: Inventing lower costs for the preferred option.
Ignoring every implementation constraint.
Using the same relevant criteria for both options.
Changing the criteria to favour one option.
check.explanation: Consistent criteria let the reader assess the trade-off.

lessons.title: Balanced conclusions
lessons.explanation: A balanced conclusion weighs the evidence rather than giving equal weight to every view. State the most defensible judgement and the conditions or uncertainty that remain.
lessons.example: A limited trial may be preferable if supervision is feasible; otherwise a different arrangement needs consideration.

check.prompt: Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?
options: The trial is defensible if the staffing condition can be met.
Every view is equally supported regardless of evidence.
The trial is certain to solve every problem.
No conclusion is ever possible.
check.explanation: It takes a position while retaining a relevant condition.

lessons.title: Constructing an analytical paragraph
lessons.explanation: Develop a controlling judgement, explain a mechanism, examine an alternative, state evidence needs and reach a qualified conclusion. A list of facts is insufficient.
lessons.example: Outline only: issue → mechanism → competing explanation → evidence needed → conditional judgement. The writer supplies the analysis.

check.prompt: Which element changes a descriptive list into analysis?
options: Using longer words without clearer reasoning.
Explaining and testing relationships between the observations.
Adding more unexplained facts.
Repeating the issue title.
check.explanation: Analysis depends on reasoned relationships and evidence, not length.
